extracted.intended_audience: ERC grant applicants (especially those who received an Evaluation Summary Report after rejection)
extracted.subtask_description: How to interpret an ERC Evaluation Summary Report (ESR) after a rejected application: categorize reviewer comments, decide which criticisms require revision, whether to resubmit or file redress, and how to revise presentation and scientific concept for future ERC deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of reading the ESR
rubrics_metrics.description: The main purpose of reading the ESR is getting professional feedback about the project and understanding if the reason for rejection precludes the project from reapplying in consecutive deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the ESR to diagnose whether the criticism is fixable (so you can reapply) or fundamental (may preclude reapplication). Comments may also motivate you to file a redress when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group I — Highly important comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually refer directly to the scientific content and concept of the project, or to the suggested methodology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectively assess whether the reviewer was right. If correct, revise the project's concept and/or scientific presentation accordingly. If you believe the comment is incorrect, carefully reconsider the proposal's presentation and how to defend the scientific concept to avoid repeating such criticism. Check how many reviewers repeated the same issue—repetition indicates higher severity. Remember external reviewers are independent; carefully address criticism on scientific merit that repeats more than once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group II — “Nice to have” comments
rubrics_metrics.description: These comments tend to be more technical, and normally do not serve as main reasons for disqualification of an ERC grant application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether more than one reviewer mentions the specific comment—single-reviewer technical comments 'weigh' less. After collecting these comments, consider which ones to address in the new application and how; it is not always recommended to attend to all comments in this group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group III — Irrelevant / Unexplained / Unjustified / Personal comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments which do not reflect the essence of ERC and may come from uninformed reviewers; they tend to be unfair and unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review these carefully, but in most cases the advice is to ignore this type of comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check repetition of criticisms across reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine how many reviewers repeated a specific comment to assess its severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple reviewers independently raise the same concern, treat it as a serious issue requiring careful revision; single-reviewer comments generally carry less weight. Use repetition as a signal when prioritizing which criticisms to address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider filing a redress when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments from the ESR may motivate you to file a redress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you identify unjustified or procedurally problematic comments (or other grounds indicated by ESR), evaluate whether a formal redress is appropriate and timely according to ERC procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resubmission strategy (do not copy & paste)
rubrics_metrics.description: Resubmission is not simply copy & paste of the previous proposal; ERC is a highly competitive grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully review the ESR and consider comments, criticism, personal and career considerations. Decide whether the project is 'ERC material' or needs further improvement, modification, and adjustments. If you reapply, give the application process careful attention and explicitly address prior criticisms rather than reusing the previous text unchanged.
